utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the ammunition that was found in the grave, can we assume, therefore, that there were high-calibre weapons there, 30 millimetres, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does your overall image of the grave site exclude the possibility that in this trench at this position with the heavy-calibre weaponry, that there was shooting going on during combat operations and that the ammunition that was found in fact represents part of those activities and operations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes and no. If I may explain the no part of it that would be in my opinion. I do agree with the fact that to fire a 30-millimetre round, you cannot do that from a handgun or a rifle. It has to be a quite substantially large gun. Therefore, those shells found at the bottom of the trench, one of which was smashed, as a matter of fact, could be linked to the fact that whenever this gun in transport or carrying this gun or whatever was moving this gun may have smashed some shell casings left behind. However, I do not see what would be the use, in my opinion, to fire a 30-millimetre weapon together with a 7.65-millimetre pistol bullet. If I was firing a 30-millimetre weapon that would have a very long range, I presume, I would not expect my pistol to reach as far as the other weapon. That is my first, in my opinion, objection. The second one is that why would I have then a body lying in a gun emplacement? We do know two things regarding this. In the picture that was shown to you that is Exhibit number -- if I can find it here -- OTP Exhibit 14/10 of the 27th of July, we see that the site labelled as NK-7 is still open, is very much an empty -- an empty trench. So the point is that we know that whatever happened there has to happen, according to this photograph, after the 27th of July. The problem with the shell casings is, just to summarise this, is that 30-millimetre shell casings and a handgun, in my opinion, are not something that are really compatible in terms of, let's say, fighting of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the interpretation was not the proper one, but on page 17 of your report, we don't mention a shell casing but just a bullet. No mention is made of a shell casing, which means that somebody dropped a bullet in the trench.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not follow you. You may repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 16. I'm sorry. On page 16 of your report. I see that it is page 16 now. You make no mention of the shell casing of a pistol, of a 7.62-millimetre pistol, but the complete bullet, which leads me to conclude that somebody lost the bullet in the trench rather than having shot from the trench with a pistol. On the other hand -- to round off my question, on the other hand, you found shell casings of 7.62-millimetre automatic weapons, which leads me to conclude that if somebody did, in fact, fire, were using weapons other than heavy weapons, he fired only from an automatic weapon of the 7.62-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your first point, the 7.65-millimetre pistol bullet is, indeed, a bullet, and is not a live round, is a fired bullet; otherwise, it would be referring to a round. It is a bullet and therefore has been fired. Then we have, on top of it, three shell casings of 7.62 millimetres, and we've got two bullets, again fired rounds, of 7.62 millimetres and a jacket fragment, the part of the bullet that encases the core of the bullet, that we cannot determine from where it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the body was found next to the place where the projectiles were uncovered -- at least that is what is shown on your sketch on figure number 5 -- does that exclude the possibility of the fact that it was a body which had previously been hit and later on introduced into the trench?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have really no, again, opinion about it. The answer again could be "yes". However, by the same token, I could, in my opinion, question why then those fired bullets are in the sediment in close proximity to the body. But the answer to your question would be "yes".

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question relates to the next grave site, Konjevic Polje. I'm sorry, Nova Kasaba 08, that is the next grave site. In this grave, you explained to us that you found 33 individuals who were buried in three groups, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your conclusion in paragraph 3 seems to indicate that the groups -- that the individuals in the first and third groups were shot in the grave itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Also, your conclusion in paragraph 4 indicates that clusters 1 and 2 were mechanically removed from an unknown location and disposed of in the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that there is something illogical there. If cluster 1 was mechanically removed from an unknown location and then buried in the grave, why was that same cluster shot at in the Nova Kasaba 8 grave itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have not stated the answer to that question because it will be too much to speculate. But in my opinion, if I may, I would speculate regarding this in order to answer the question. There are two things that need to be taken into account. If I'm saying that the bodies were transported mechanically, it's because we have physical evidence linking turf, meaning grass, under the bodies as if they've been scooped. That is a fact. There is no interpretation linking that fact to anything else. So my interpretation goes, then, to the mechanical removal of the bodies. That is number 1. Number 2, I have never said in any point in time whether the people were scooped alive or dead because I cannot make that interpretation. Again, if somebody has bullets under the body embedded in the ground, I am only saying that the person may have been shot while in the grave. I am not saying whether the person has been killed while in the grave, nor whether the person has been killed elsewhere and then transported to the grave. That is something I cannot extract, assess, nor answer based on the evidence I have recovered. So the facts basically are that the mechanical removal is one thing, primarily supported by the fact of the grass and the turf and the sediment under the bodies. And the second element is that through all those sediments, there are bullets, and on some occasions I stated in the report -- not in this specific case, I believe -- there has been an association between injuries recorded by the pathologist and the position of the bullets. So I'm leaving all this here very purposely vague in order not to over-interpret my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, at what depth below the bodies were the projectiles found? Do you have that fact?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me look for it in the report. It only says here that three to four bullets and one jacket fragment -- that's referring to cluster 1 -- were found embedded in the bottom of the grave. Again, I would say that by "embedded", I mean the bullet was literally stuck in the ground, in the soil, below the depth of at least half an inch or over a centimetre to an inch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, one more question relating to this grave. As we're in the area of speculation, there is something one might call a custom, a rather strange one. In wartime, it has been recorded on many occasions that bodies that have died and that are thrown into a grave, a burst of fire, a round of fire, is fired in order to confirm I don't really know what. And bearing in mind, in particular, the conclusions you make regarding grave site Nova Kasaba 8 -- and my question is related to the previous graves -- could this possibility be excluded, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me rephrase, only for the sake of understanding, to see if I understand your question. What you suggest is that in wartimes, a burst of fire may be open against an individual that is already placed into a grave for some reason. I just need clarification on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer would be, no, I am not acquainted with that information you have produced. However, in my opinion again, I would say that if somebody opens a burst of fire against a body lying on a grave, it is because that person suspects that the individual may still be alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My next question relates to the Konjevic Polje 1 grave site. Within the framework of this grave, you registered the presence of a white powder?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The existence of this white powder, could it be an indication that it was scattered in order to prevent possible disease from spreading?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, in my opinion again -- I cannot answer this question if I don't give an explanation for it. It is, in my opinion again, lime, in general, is placed in graves in any country in the world primarily to quench smell more than to prevent disease, as far as I know. I don't really see what disease-preventing capabilities lime has for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does lime itself have a smell?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lime, in itself, does not have a smell such as the one that it's trying to quench, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In that connection, is it a fact that most of the bodies were transported mechanically, by mechanical means? At least that is what I gather from your report.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, at least those to be buried first, the first eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: One of the reasons -- I'm not just referring to this grave but the others too. Most of the bodies were transported mechanically to the grave sites; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have evidence that in some instances, as I have put in my report, some bodies or some groups of bodies were transported mechanically to the location where they were buried, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could one of the reasons be fear of infection or -- could one of the reasons be fear of infection, or the unpleasant stench, could that be one of the explanations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be one of the explanations for burying the bodies, not for them being transported mechanically, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My next question -- just a moment, please. There's another question I have to ask. Does lime, in contact with water, emanate a particular smell?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question relates to the Konjevic Polje 2 grave site. According to your finding, this grave was dug by hand?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Both graves were dug by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But still there are traces that the body was mechanically put into the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct for grave 1 and maybe for one individual in grave 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is this grave an instance of the kind of speculation we referred to earlier on as to the reasons for putting bodies into the grave by mechanical means?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. However, I would like to clarify this issue a bit more. In my report, I say that the grave in grave 1, for example, was dug by hand, and that individual may have been placed there through mechanical means because it was lying on a pedestal of turf, branches and some flowers. What I'm not saying in my report, however, is when the hole in which the body was placed was open -- in other words, a hole becomes a grave by putting a body in it. I do not know and there's no way I can know whether the hole was simply a hole and has been there for a long time and then a body was placed in it later. So that just helps to clarify, in that specific case, that I'm not trying to infer when -- or why, rather, or to speculate why, if I open a grave by hand or I dig a grave by hand, why I put in a body mechanically. I cannot really speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have several more questions for the witness, but I am looking at the time. I don't know whether it might be advisable to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. Do you have any idea how much more time you need to finish your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another ten minutes or so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes or so? I think we should have a break then. So we're going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, you may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, let us go on to the next grave site, Glogova. In view of the global impression you have of this grave site, would you agree that there were several burials in that grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as regards the time when those burials took place?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. From the direct examination of the graves, I do not have an impression of the time. Having said that, I do have an impression of the time based on the photographs showed to me by the investigators, that have already been presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Regarding this grave and in view of the bodies recovered, can it be said that bodies were brought to this grave from several locations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is actually possible for any grave, including this one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your report, you said that a person was found with a Baretta pistol on him.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how that individual was clothed?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the pathology report again -- it's in my notes -- he was dressed with a black leather jacket, green tartan shirt, olive-green T-shirt, and brown trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could this be described as civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this grave, a group of bodies was found with traces of scorching. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I think that we should tell the Court that we're referring to GL-05 specifically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I guess that that matter will be dealt with when the pathologist -- with the pathologist's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this grave, a certain quantity of lime was also found, as was the case in the previous graves.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you say that there was a particular reason for this?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what is the reason of putting the lime there. I just know that there was quite a lot of it, as much as -- I would say almost a cubic metre. Quite a lot of lime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, within the framework of your studies and investigations, you managed to obtain a global overview of virtually all the graves.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If the existence of lime could be a reason for concealing a grave, how would you explain that in the case of secondary grave sites lime is mostly absent, with the exception of Zeleni Jadar 5?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to answer your question in my opinion, because I have never discussed that issue in any of my reports. In my opinion, lime is not a means of concealing a grave. I would conceal a grave by backfilling it with something else less visible from the surface. And as a matter of fact, in the report, I said that at least 75 centimetres of the area where the grave was supposed to be, 65, sorry, centimetres, was disturbed. So when we arrive to the area, the only visible thing would have shown in photograph 15 in my report, page 34, was basically an overgrown area. When digging that, we have to remove 65 or more centimetres of soil that had been just ploughed over and over. Even after that, when we recovered the cut or the area, the extent of the grave, we found the lime. Therefore, the lime was part of the grave but, in my opinion, was not to be used to conceal anything. It was simply there for whatever other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. Mr. Baraybar, thank you for your detailed answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have only a few questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Baraybar, in your examination-in-chief you were referred -- and indeed in your cross-examination -- you were referred to Exhibit 232, which is the addendum to your report and sets out the minimum number of individuals and their age groups from the various sites on which you reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 140, and specifically page 00950927.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, I want you to concentrate on the diagram on the extreme right of that page, which is the Orahovac/Lezete 2 and then linked to Hodzici Road 3, Hodzici Road 4 and Hodzici Road 5. When you wrote your report in December of 1999, were you aware that examination of shell cases and blindfolds and ligatures had linked Orahovac/Lezete 2 with the secondary sites at Hodzici Road 3, Hodzici Road 4, and Hodzici Road 5?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only evidence that I have used for those links, as called in my report, have been the pollen and soil analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you were not aware of that subsequent evidence that's been discovered since your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Since the writing of your report, you're not aware of that new evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to the Nova Kasaba 4 site and specifically your exhumation report that is on page 7, you state, in the second paragraph of your summary and conclusions, that there were two adult males with mean ages of 17 years. Now, you're not stating in this report that those two individuals were actually 17 years of age, are you?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by "mean age of 17"?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mean" is a measure of a central tendency. In other words, if I have an individual that, according to my analysis, is between -- let's just take a hypothetical example -- between 20 and 30, I would say that its mean age is 25. I am not saying, however, that he is 25. He is somewhere between 20 and 30. The problem is that in terms of writing a report, if I am to explain or refer to ranges all the time, it would be extremely confusing. In that case, it's basically why I'm using a mean age of 17 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So am I right in saying that explains why, in your anthropological report, you used age ranges, but in order to make a more realistic presentation in your exhumations report, you used a mean age of 17?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and the mean age -- the mean of 17 is roughly the mean of the range 13 to 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could refer you to page 11 of your report, and this is simply a clarification, you state that a young adult male, in the second paragraph of that page of your report, was found with 54 7.62-millimetre live rounds. Were they actually found on his person or were they found nearby to the body?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, they were in close association to the body. I'm not making any reference here, although I can check my notes if you give me a minute. Yes. The bullets were in close association. There's no mention of a pouch, there's no mention of anything. They were not, let's say, a metre or ten centimetres away from the body. They were on the body. Therefore, they are associated to the body. I am not saying, however -- that's why I have not stated here -- that the body was carrying that, because there was found no carrying case or bag or anything. It was simply associated to the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Since you've been asked in your cross-examination to exclude a number of possibilities, and I don't want you to speculate, can you exclude the possibility that those rounds of ammunition were thrown on top of the body after the body was put into the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move to Nova Kasaba 8 and page 20 of your report, you were asked a number of questions about bullets -- deformed bullets that were found under a number of bodies, and you state in your report that the three bullets, the 7.62-millimetre bullets, were found in the soil deformed. Question: Is it right that when bullets pass through bodies and hit flesh or bone, that they deform or flatten?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And by deforming or flattening, does that reduce the distance that they can travel once they have left the body?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were asked -- and this is really my final question in respect of Nova Kasaba 4 -- whether you could exclude the possibility that the individuals in that grave were killed in combat, and your answer was, in essence, that you could not but that there were a number of factors which went against drawing that conclusion. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge of that grave, equally can you exclude the possibility, Mr. Baraybar, that the individuals in that grave were summarily executed and then placed in that grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Good morning, Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I've been listening very carefully to your testimony. I have a general question, in fact, related to the cross-examination and to what our Prosecutor has just asked you. When you were asked by the distinguished Defence counsel if some casualties could have happened during combat, your answer was, "No," and you gave reasons. You said that some carried stretchers, some were reported missing by the ICRC, some had dressings of previous wound shots. Does this apply to all the mass grave sites, or were there some which indicated a battle connected with it, or were some traces of military clothes, weapons, around or in the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding the first example, that is, Nova Kasaba 4, as I said, we recovered 19 individuals and two stretchers. Three individuals were with some kind of dressing. One of them specifically had a splint. They wear different items of clothing and other objects. In this specific case, the only military element, if I can call it in another way, although I'm speculating because we would need to define what military items are, the obvious military item would be the live rounds that were found in the grave. In the grave of Glogova as well, we found a pistol, a loaded pistol being directly carried, not put in the grave but carried by an individual. In general terms, I do not recall any other obviously military elements such as camouflage fatigues, khaki trousers, gun holsters or other elements of military paraphernalia that were found in the graves, helmets. The range would be limited. So the answer is, basically, we have only -- we can not exclude -- I cannot exclude to a hundred per cent the fact whether they would be military casualties or not. My evidence does not allow me to over-interpret beyond what I have. But in sort of physical evidence, we have only those two instances I have referred to as the most military things that could have been found, rounds and a loaded pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned that one of the bodies had bullets almost on the body. Now, if a body is thrown in a grave dug, would he fall with the bullets over him?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 54 bullets we were referring to in the case of Nova Kasaba 4 were four groups of bullets placed on a -- on a clip. So it was a package of bullets in there. I do not know -- the bullets were not, let's say, spread all over the body. There was a tight package of bullets, because bullets were in these clips, held in a clip. So they were not thrown, they were in a package. The issue is whether the body was carrying those bullets. I cannot say for sure. What I have said is there was no bag, there was no suitcase, no backpack, no nothing in which the bullets were found. So the body was here, and the bullets were literally attached to the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: With a belt?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Baraybar, you mentioned that in one of the graves, I think it was Konjevic Polje 1, there was a body of a woman, and I believe that was the only identified woman found in all of the graves that you included in your report. Was there anything at all unusual or anything, from your point of view, that would explain the presence of that lone woman in the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no -- again, my evidence does not allow me to speculate as to why she was there. However, there's something I can definitely comment upon, and it's the fact that from the remains that have been classified as undetermined by different causes, either, because they were very fragmented, there were tiny pieces, none of them, the ones that were more or less complete, showed female features or obvious features of a female. The interesting factor here is that during the exhumation, all the field team, upon having a close look at the body said, "This is a woman." I was the most skeptical person, maybe influenced by the fact that in the past we have been dealing with hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of male victims to actually accept that this was a female. Well, it was a female. We had a cursory look in the field, and then I was able to re-examine the body in the mortuary. It was a full skeleton, and indeed it was a female. On top of it, as far as I can recall, it had some pink trainer shoes, and I can't really recall the rest of the clothing, but it was quite a striking element for other people than me, so to speak. They just saw it and said, "This is a female. It is a female." My impression was maybe it's not. Maybe it was a dressed as a male, but it was definitely a female.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was there anything in that relatively small grave site to suggest that the female had been -- had met her death in any different way than the males?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I again would leave comments on the cause of death of the female to the chief pathologist. I am going through my report. Well, apparently she was shot. The pathologist would be able to explain that better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My second question deals with the phenomenon that's been so extensively discussed of those bodies that you found in a few different sites where at least you said in the beginning they would be consistent with the person having been shot when they were already in the grave, although other possibilities were discussed. Could you tell, from the evidence that you look at, if that were true, if that possibility that you first mentioned were true, that the body was shot while in the grave, that these bodies had been tossed into the grave and then shot or that they had actually been, as it were, ordered into the grave and then shot while they were still active and upright?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the individuals in grave 2 in the site of Konjevic Polje 2, KP-02, may answer this question. This body happened to have three 7.62-millimetre bullets embedded in the grave floor under the body. One was below the waist, at the chest level, and the right shoulder. In both cases, the second body in the same grave has also a bullet under the chest. I wrote in my report here that according to the pathologist's report, the cause of death of both individuals was multiple gunshot wounds. The pathologist will explain this in detail. However, the interesting fact is, and this is extracted from the pathologist's report, so this is not my examination but the pathologist's examination, in both cases the location of the bullets matched the injuries recorded during the post-mortem examination. So up to there, I can say that in this specific case, I have a link, an independent link between the bullets being found under the bodies and the pathologist's examination. It is a separate examination from the one I did when I recovered the bodies and the locations have both matched. Whether the person was forced in there or not is something very difficult to ascertain, extremely difficult to ascertain. However, if some people, such as the Defence counsel asked me previously, where a burst of gunfire was opened on them while in the grave and they were transported mechanically, well, I would not like to draw the conclusion of that, but it seems to me very obvious that if somebody does that, it's because the person is not dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question to you is: In the final part of your direct-examination, you were shown Exhibit 140, which showed the sites that have already been exhumed and those that have not yet been exhumed. Do you know of any schedule or what the schedule will be? In short, how much longer it is likely to be, number of years before those sites, if they are going to be exhumed, can be exhumed?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Baraybar, I also have a few questions for you, at least five brief questions, in actual fact. You talk about -- you talked about American standards, Bosnian standards for calculating age. Now, even for the American standard, does it require -- how shall I put this? -- continuously examines in order to maintain the viability of the standard?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a certain extent that is correct. Beyond that, I would tell you that if a sample is large enough and representative -- more than large -- large and representative, that would be the right combination. The standard can stand on its own. Some adjustments would need to be made if the sample is under-represented in some parts, but otherwise, the technique itself will be standing on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These same statistical operations, are they applied to perform the adaptations of the American norm to the Bosnian standard or are there different operations to do this?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is the same -- it is basically the same operation. As I explained, the features to be observed remain the same. What changes is the number of individuals that share those features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In applying the standard, let us say Bosnian, have you maintained the same criteria throughout, for numerous observations or did you change the criteria?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we made -- we were made aware in 1999 of this study, what we have done is we have changed the ranges, not the observations, of the previous years. Well, not the previous years. I correct that. Only of 1998, because 1996 was already presented as a report. So we have left the observations, and we have just changed the age ranges to make them more accurate, more close to reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the age groups, these ranges that you adopted, do they have any connection with the stages of human development, that is to say, children, adolescents, younger people, adults, the elderly, something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The standards we have discussed are only to age -- adult individuals in a post-development time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question for you. You compiled your report, and of course you make a report in order to answer certain questions posed. You don't do an academic report, but you do a report according to the needs. Now, can you tell me what the questions were that guided you, that the people seeking answers asked you? That is to say, what was the objective of your answers and response either in the report itself or the research applied?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It primarily was to establish a demographic profile of the population we were dealing with. So the questions asked, basically, by the investigators would be how old they are, how many they are, and what sex they are. Other things have also been performed, such as stature estimation. However, stature is something less linked to the Prosecution than to humanitarian and identification matters. We have also been recording, in addition to that, any other features; for example, if somebody may have an old fracture or things of the kind that could assist in the identification of these individuals. But again those things are not part of the report primarily because they are not pertinent to the matters we're dealing with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have made a series of speculations, which is quite acceptable in my mind if you have an expert witness, of course. It is a little difficult to distinguish the result of the observation and the opinion of the expert himself, and entering into that realm, I should like to ask you the following question. We have already associated mechanical resources used, and the smell, and possible disease. Can we associate the use of mechanical resources to rapidity, the need to be quick, and organisational needs and requirements?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, I think we can, and I'll give you some examples. In every -- take the issue of the lime or the alleged lime, the white substance. At least on two occasions, meaning the Glogova sites, the amount of it has been far beyond what one person can actually carry. A cubic metre is a substantial amount. So again unless we have 1.000 people bring a small bag, it has to be brought in a big lump and just left there. The fact that some or many -- or the majority, for that matter, of graves -- not the ones that contained one person or two people -- were dug mechanically and the fact that some of the bodies were also collected, it seems, mechanically, I would say, in my opinion, they are associated and involve definite logistics, because by experience, from my own operations, I know that it requires logistics to bring a machine. Even for us to do the work, it involves logistics. An element of time is definitely present, because if I need to bury 33 people and I have a shovel, it will take much longer than if I have a mechanical excavator, and organisation, in a way, because in my opinion I would need to know where to dig. I don't want to go to a place where there's already a grave and open it up and the bodies may have been lying there for a week, and it will be very stinky and very unpleasant. So those things, I think, are linked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Baraybar. I think that you have answered all our questions and queries from the Bench, the Prosecution, and the Defence, and this concludes your testimony, I think. Mr. Cayley, I think we have some documents to tender into evidence before the witness leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could apply for formal admission of Exhibit 220, which is the curriculum vitae of Mr. Baraybar; Exhibit 224, which is a photographic copy of a male pelvic bone; Exhibit 225, which is the female pelvis; 226, which is the skull; 227, which is the calculation of the minimum number of individuals; 229 is the same diagram but where it involves a primary and secondary site; 230, which is the table of age distribution for long bones; 231, a table of age distribution of long bones; 232 is an addendum to the anthropological report; 233 is the anthropological report; 234 is the exhumation report, and then the final exhibit is the sketch that Mr. Baraybar did, which is Exhibit 161/2/A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents have therefore been admitted. Now we should like to thank you, Mr. Baraybar, for coming here, for your cooperation with international justice, and we wish you every success in your future work. And unfortunately there is always scope for that work. The usher will now escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, what are we going to do now? We have a problem. We have had two breaks. Perhaps it's a bit much to go on until 2.30, and perhaps we could now have a quarter of an hour break and then go on working until 2.30. What do you have for us, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We do have another witness for the Court, Mr. President. We have a forensic pathology, as you could probably predict. His examination-in-chief will be longer than an hour; not much longer than an hour, but certainly longer than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, perhaps I could ask the registrar to have the witness brought in. We will have a 15-minute break, and then we will resume with the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have Dr. John Clark with us. Good afternoon. You're going to read the solemn declaration, which the usher is handing to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Dr. Clark, I think you are familiar with proceedings in the courtroom, so I'm sure you will be quite at ease. For the moment, you're going to answer questions put to by Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, before we begin your evidence, something that we have spoken about, you and I are both speaking English.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Between us are banks of highly-skilled interpreters, but because we speak the same language, it makes their task more difficult. If you can speak as slowly as you can, and I will try and regulate the pace, and also if you can take a pause after my question before you answer and I will do the same. That will make life easier for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your name is John Clark; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were born on the 5th of September, 1951?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're British. You're a Scotsman, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've a bachelor's degree in medicine and surgery from the University of Aberdeen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are, by profession and specialisation, a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you've lectured in forensic pathology at the Universities of Aberdeen, Sheffield, and Glasgow, and you're currently teaching at the University of Glasgow.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the University of Glasgow has one of the major academic departments in the United Kingdom on forensic pathology and certainly the largest?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're a fellow of the Royal College of Pathologists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court what that means.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Essentially, any doctor in the United Kingdom wanting to qualify as a pathologist has to pass an examination set by the Royal College of Pathologists. So I have passed that. After a certain period of time, one is made a fellow of the Royal College.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed I think you're now the chairman of the panel of examiners of the Royal College of Pathologists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: In the speciality of forensic pathology, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're also the secretary of the British Association of Forensic Medicine. Can you explain to the Judges what that role entails?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's a national association of forensic pathologists. It includes just about all forensic pathologists in the United Kingdom. We also have many members from other countries. We meet, have academic meetings twice a year and other activities, and I'm the general secretary of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, apart from your academic duties, can you describe to the Judges your profession obligations, like how many autopsies you perform every year, the geographical extent of your forensic pathology specialisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Carrying out post-mortems is, in fact, the largest component of my work. I carry out probably 350 to 400 post-mortem examinations every year. That is involving a very wide range of deaths, from natural disease but including a substantial number of homicides and other suspicious deaths. My work involves working for the legal authorities in a large part of Scotland, the main population of Scotland in the Glasgow region, and occasionally elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, for the sake of the public -- the Judges are familiar with the type of work that you do -- what is a pathologist, first of all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: A pathologist is a medical doctor who, amongst other things, carries out post-mortem examinations on people who have died to try and find out why they have died. A forensic pathologist, in particular, is someone who deals with people who have died in suspicious or criminal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Apart from your work at the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, where else have you worked? And I'm speaking now in the international context.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I have substantial work with the Tribunal both in Bosnia and in Croatia. I have also carried out a post-mortem examination in Pakistan on a chief of the army general staff, and last year I was briefly in Kosovo carrying out post-mortem examinations on two Albanians who had been allegedly shot by British soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, I'm not going to go through the whole of your curriculum vitae. It speaks for itself in terms of your work, your publications, and indeed your international work. I would simply offer it to the Court as Exhibit 235. Now, I think I'm right in saying that you worked on the Srebrenica investigation in connection with your autopsy work as a pathologist in 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, not in 1996, 1998 for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, in 1998. And then you assisted as a pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In 1999, I think you were the chief pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you have in front of you, I think, your report from that season. We'll be referring to it. It's going to be Prosecutor's Exhibit 236. Do you have a copy in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, because it's a matter that has arisen before, who worked for you and with you in the mortuary in the 1999 season?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It was quite a large team of individuals, pathologists, anthropologists, technicians, a radiographer, scenes-of-crime officers, and other assistants. They were drawn from many different countries of the world. In fact, we had nineteen countries represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Exhibit 238 could be placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Or, indeed, if you have it, Dr. Clark, with you. Sir, these represent a pretty good cross-section of member states of the United Nations. Staff were drawn from all of these countries who worked with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And did that work well, Dr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It worked very well. Obviously, everyone had their own medical-legal backgrounds and were used to carrying out examinations in different ways. But we had a fairly common standard, and everything did work very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can move on to the operation at the mortuary, and if you could -- I know it's covered in your report, but if you could describe firstly to the Judges briefly how you received bodies and parts of bodies into the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I think the bulk of the evidence you've heard so far has been related to the grave sites. The bodies were removed from the graves and put in individual body bags. These were then stored in a refrigerator at the site. Regularly, that refrigerator was brought down to the mortuary. The bodies were transferred from it into a large refrigerated room in the mortuary. This was all carefully logged, and the bodies were stored in the room until the post-mortem examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To your knowledge, and if you're aware, was the chain of custody or evidence in respect to the bodies closely monitored by members of the staff?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, including myself. We all took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could explain briefly to the Judges how the mortuary operated, so the process that you went through, and the pathologists that worked for you, in actually examining the body and making a report on the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Briefly, the body would be removed from the refrigerator and the numbers logged on various worksheets. The first step in examination was to fluoroscope the body. This is a form of X-ray which just scans over the whole body and is looking for fragments of metal and particularly bullets. This has two uses. It indicates that there are bullets present in the body, which is -- and we can make a permanent record of that on a printout, and secondly it assists us knowing exactly where it is in the examination, and we can then find it all the more easily. That's the first step. Then the bodies are taken to the examination tables themselves, and various procedures are then carried out, including photography, both at the start and during the examinations. We removed the clothing, and this was washed -- subsequently washed, and we described it in detail later on. We removed any blindfolds or ligatures on the body. We looked for any possessions or any other identifying items such as documents, jewellery, etc. Then the main part of the examination, from the point of view of the pathologist, was to examine the body for various things, its state of preservation, any parts missing, identifying features like hair colour present, height, any old injuries, age, et cetera. Then particularly we looked for injuries on the body and made a careful record of these, and also looked for any natural disease which was present. In doing all this, we retrieved bullets and any bullet fragments, and these were handed to the scenes-of-crime officers, and we collected various samples particularly for future DNA testing. We were assisted in the work by technicians and particularly by anthropologists, and they helped us to establish identifying features like age, height, sex, and also assisted in reconstructing bones and interpretation of injuries. And the final thing that we, as pathologists, did was to look at the clothing again after it had been washed. This was all recorded on to a pro forma, a post-mortem report form, so each pathologist completed that in longhand and it was subsequently typed up into a final autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just place on the ELMO Exhibit 237. Now, this is an example of an autopsy report that you completed. We'll talk about it in more detail when we come to the relevant site. Did you review all of the autopsy reports that were produced by pathologists working with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I should perhaps just say, because this doesn't look particularly impressive -- there's a lot of scoring out -- this is the rough copy which we completed, and it comprises about eight or nine pages. It's recording all the details, et cetera. And then the final report typed up is what you see on the front page, two- or three-page report. So that's how it ends up. At the end of the season, I went through all the reports and extracted various bits of information and analysed them and put them into this final report, which is presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So essentially your report is a comprehensive summary of all of the autopsy reports from the 1999 season?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, in your report, you address the limitations of pathology evidence in this type of case, and I wonder if you could explain to the Judges what those limitations are in a case such as this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Obviously, we were not dealing with ideal conditions and ideal bodies; certainly not the sort of bodies that we, as pathologists, normally deal with. Primarily, this was because these were bodies which had been dead for a number of years, had decomposed very badly, and had been disrupted for various reasons. So that made things difficult, for a start. If I can just concentrate on perhaps four specific areas of difficulty and how we approached them. The first one was actually recognising that something that we found was an injury and that it was an injury caused in life. In a person who's died recently, when we examine the body looking for injuries, we can tell that injuries happened in life because of various reactions; bleeding, swelling, bruising, et cetera, on the body. And that allows us to say that that is an ante-mortem injury. Clearly, when a body is decomposed or there are no tissues left at all, then we don't have that evidence. And in the vast majority of cases here, all we were left with was the skeleton and just injuries to bone. Now, an injury to bone will look exactly the same if it's caused before death as it is caused after death, and it is really only by looking at these other things like bruising and bleeding, et cetera, that we can be sure that that is caused in life. So, theoretically, given that these bodies were almost all skeletonised, we could not 100 per cent say that any of these injuries occurred in life. But we had to be rather sensible about this. These bodies had huge numbers of gunshot injuries, and if we were to suggest that all these injuries occurred after death, then we're suggesting that all these people died in some obscure way that we had not detected and also that they had been shot afterwards, systematically shot after death. So on that basis, finding that unbelievable, we adopted the position that any injuries suggestive of gunshot damage, we assumed, with the occasional exception, we assumed had occurred in life. The second area was that we knew that there was damage -- there would have been damage to the bodies, injuries to the bodies after death. This is because these bodies were, a large number of them, lumped in a grave, piled on top of each other. You will get crushing effect. There may also have been vehicles on top of the grave compacting the bodies. So it was to be expected that we would find injuries caused after death. We could usually recognise for what they were, because the sort of injuries we would expect would be crushing injuries of the ribs, which are the most brittle bones. Crushing injuries of the pelvis because it splits open under pressure. And indeed many of the bodies did have injuries like this. So we interpreted these injuries as having occurred after death. That may have meant that we missed genuine injuries, blunt-force injuries, but we just had to accept that. So we interpreted this crushing type of injuries of the chest and pelvis as having occurred after death. The third area, and I'll be brief, given the bulk of the evidence here, was gunshot injuries, how did we prove that a particular damage to a bone was a gunshot injury and not something else. And we worked on varying levels of certainty that this was gunshot damage. Clearly if there was a very typical bullet entrance in the bone, that was classic evidence of a gunshot injury, entrance and exit perhaps. Alternatively, we may just have had a very fragmented piece of bone. That, again, highly typical of gunshot damage, high-velocity gunshot damage, and it may have been backed up by finding, perhaps, some bullet fragments with it. The third proof of gunshot damage may have been that we actually found a bullet or part of a bullet in tissues in the body, and that, again, clearly is proof that there's been a shot to the body. Without that, without any of these three categories, although we perhaps might suspect that a particular injury was gunshot damage, we didn't call it that because we didn't have the full proof it. So again, we may well have underestimated the number of gunshot injuries to the body. The fourth area of limitation in our evidence is accepting what is and what isn't a cause of death. This was proving that a particular injury to the body necessarily killed the person, because again, we're left -- we just have the skeleton to deal with. People don't die because of damage to the skeleton. You die of the damage to the associated tissues round about, the damage to the organs, to the blood vessels, et cetera. With decomposed bodies that evidence is gone, so we're left just to speculate as to what damage there would have been or there possibly could have been based on what we found on the bones. Now, I think it's reasonable to suggest that a bullet going through somebody's skull is also going to go through their brain. You don't die of the damage to the skull, you die of the damage to the brain, but we felt it was reasonable to assume that that would -- that there would have been damage, fatal damage, to the brain. Similarly, a bullet striking the chest, I think that it's safe to assume that that would have caused fatal damage to the major organs as blood vessels in the chest, and it is highly likely that one or more of them would have been damaged. The difficulty came when all we had was perhaps an injury to an arm or a leg, a gunshot injury to the arm or leg. An injury like that would not necessarily be fatal. It could be if it damaged a large blood vessel in the leg, the person may bleed to death, but we could not prove that. These are potentially survivable injuries. So if that was the only injuries we found on the body, by and large we felt that we cannot, in all honesty, say that that was necessarily the cause of death, so we tended to leave these causes of death unascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, even taking into account all of these limitations that you rightfully identify, how did the vast majority of these people die, in your professional opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The vast majority died of gunshot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could place Exhibit 195 onto the overhead projector. That's correct. That's the one. Just to orient the Court and the public, what is represented by the orange shading on these particular sites?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That is the grave site I was involved in. So the main one was Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, the two Konjevic Polje graves, and finally Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And these are the sites on which you acted as the chief pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could move now to Kozluk, and you might wish to turn to the relevant page in your report to assist your recollection, how many whole or largely complete bodies did you examine from this site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We found 292 whole or largely complete bodies, and there were an additional 233 body parts. By "body parts," I'm meaning what it says really, part of a body but perhaps a forearm or some leg bones or a few ribs. Just a fairly small part of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the figure of 292 actually represents the number of people that were originally in that grave.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I'm sure there were more individuals, yes. Two hundred and ninety-two is certainly a minimum number, and most of my calculations are based on the 292, because it's only with the largely complete bodies that one can make reasonable interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, the anthropological conclusions on the number of individuals would be different from the figures that you have here, because you are the pathologist dealing with bodies essentially?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Our main remit was to look, to examine the bodies for injuries rather than count the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The people that you examined from Kozluk, in life what kind of people were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we know that they ranged widely in age, potentially from as young as 8 to potentially as old as 85. In Kozluk, the bulk of the people were over 25, and as far as we could determine, all were male. They were not a uniformly fit group of people, and a significant number had physical disabilities or some evidence of chronic disease. For instance, and it's on --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 239 is that photograph, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This is a photograph of somebody's elbow joint, upper arm here and forearm here. Now, the elbow joint, as we all know, normally moves. This person is completely rigid. The bones are just joined, fused together, no movement whatsoever. This person would have had a fixed -- fixed elbow joint. Similarly, one man had a completely fused knee joint. The two bones at the knee joint are just stuck together. Whether that's from an old injury or from disease it was difficult to say, but, undoubtedly, he would have walked with a completely straight leg. He wouldn't have been able to bend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the witness, for the purposes of the record, is referring to Exhibit 240.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: There were other people. Somebody had a glass eye. One man had a big plate inside his skull. He'd obviously had previous surgery. Somebody had evidence of open-heart surgery, coronary artery bypass surgery. Several had old fracture -- bony fractures. One man had an inhaler, Celbutimol [phoen] inhaler for asthma and there were a number of other deformities and illnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What other items did you find on the bodies that you examined, Dr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We found various personal possessions, simple things, spectacles, cigarettes, cigarette lighters, some documents, money, and various other items.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could place Exhibit 241 onto the ELMO, which is the next exhibit that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges what this represents, this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We found a significant number of the individuals had blindfolds around their heads; and more, even more had ligatures around their hands; and some had both. This is an example of somebody with a blindfold. It's a skull. You can see the nose here, the eye sockets here and here, and this cloth blindfold tied around the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What percentage of the bodies that were examined by you and your team had blindfolds?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We found them in 44 individuals. That's about 13 per cent of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that a number of the bodies had ligatures. And if you could place on the ELMO the next Exhibit, which is 242. What comments do you have about this photograph, Dr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, we found ligatures in 140 people. That's 41 per cent of cases. This is an example, typical example of a ligature. It's a bit of cloth which has been tied, it looks around both wrists and tied in the middle there. We found the ligatures of two materials. The bulk were cloth which was all of the same material, strips of cloth all cut from the same material. Some people also had or instead had string, sort of twine binding the wrists together, and some people had both types. Apart from one man, everyone had their hands tied behind their backs. This one man had his hands tied in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, you stated earlier that the vast majority of the bodies that were examined by you and your team had gunshot injuries. What proportion of the bodies at Kozluk had gunshot injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We found definite gunshot injury in 89 per cent of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And could you establish from where those individuals, from which direction those individuals had been shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We could establish, in a certain proportion of cases, which direction they had been shot in, and particularly in looking at injuries to the head and the trunk. And looking at that, we found most often people had been shot from behind, then a significant number from the front, some from the side and some from the top, but mostly from behind. Having said that, in a substantial number of cases we could not tell the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could place the next exhibit, which is 243, and if you could explain to the Judges what is represented in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This is a very typical gunshot injury, typical of many that we found. It's a gunshot injury to the side of the skull. This is the front of the skull, the eye socket here, the cheekbone going back here, and the ear sits roundabout here. So this is a gunshot injury. When one has a circular hole in the skull, it is an entry hole. It has caused tremendous structuring of the skull, these various lines you can see going over here and up at the top. The skull has been stuck together, glued back together again to reconstruct it, but a typical gunshot injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you and your colleagues establish the type of weapon that had been used to create these gunshot injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: To our view, all these injuries were typical of high-velocity rifle weapons. We based that both on the extent of the damage, the fragmentation of the bones, and also by the finding of typical high-velocity rifle bullets in the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To give you an example of a high-velocity weapon here, we're talking about military assault weapons such as AK-47s or their variants?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the average number of shots per body where you could actually identify that somebody had been killed by gunshot injury?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: In Kozluk, it was 2.3, so people had been shot, on average, between two to three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you able to establish in any cases that people had been injured by something other than gunshot prior to death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We found two people with bandages along with the skeleton, which did suggest previous injuries, probably soft-tissue injuries. One of these was on somebody's hand and one was on their legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any other evidence -- and I know you've already stated that there are certain limitations in this field -- of blunt-force injury to any of the bodies that you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Even allowing for these limitations and expectation of crushing injuries in the grave, we found some people with fractures of the face and the shoulder blades, which did not really fit well with post-mortem injuries, and they could well have been caused by blunt-force kicking or blows from a weapon in life.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Exhibit 244, the next exhibit, could be placed onto the ELMO. Could you explain to the Judges what is represented on this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, this is an interesting case. This is the man, the same man who had the rigid leg, which I showed you earlier, and who would have walked undoubtedly with a limp with a very straight leg. He only had one injury on his body, and that was a gunshot wound to his other foot. Now, this was a relatively intact body with all parts present and with the skin still present, so we could say fairly surely that this was the -- this appeared to be the only gunshot injury on the body, and we would not say that he died from that. It would be unusual for somebody to die from a single gunshot wound to the foot. We could not find out why he died, and one could only speculate as to what may have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it possible, in your opinion, that he may have been placed alive into the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think that's entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How would he have died in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: He would -- he could have died eventually from blood loss, although it would take some time. He could have died, if he was in the grave, from crushing, suffocation under other bodies or other material. Alternatively, he could have been killed in other ways which we would not detect at post-mortem. Any cutting injuries, perhaps stabbing or cutting throats, would be difficult for us to see post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now, Dr. Clark, you could place Prosecutor's Exhibit 245, which is actually two exhibits, first of all the photograph, and there's a larger version of that next to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is an exhibit, Your Honours, that was previously addressed by Professor Wright.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, were you able to identify the autopsy reports in respect of each one of these numbered bodies in this grave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could go through each one, and if it's possible -- I know you've done a little sketch which -- would it be easier for you to have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the bodies are numbered, so I think it's quite clear if you just keep the paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. We're really speaking about these five bodies here, here, here, here, and here. And if I deal with them from right to left, it was interesting just generally that these were all young men. No one was over the age of 35, in our estimate, and some perhaps as young as 12. So the age range in all of them was 12 to 35. This one at the end, 65, he was found face down, and he had a probable single gunshot wound to the back of his neck, or to his neck, rather. Number 61, he was found with a ligature partly around his wrists. He had three gunshot injuries, one to the back of the head and two to the legs. Body 81, he had no obvious bony injuries, but we did find a bullet inside his ribcage, with staining of the bone, suggesting that the bullet had been genuinely lying there. And the pathologist felt that that was sufficient evidence to suggest that he died of a gunshot wound of the chest. Number 82 had two gunshot injuries, one to the upper chest and one to his left leg. The cause of death there was felt to be a gunshot wound to the chest. And finally to body 83, the one lying along the way, he had a single gunshot injury to the front of his left arm. This was one of these cases in which the pathologist felt he could not justifiably say that that was the cause of death and left the cause as unascertained.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, the autopsy report that we previously put into evidence is, in fact, from the Kozluk site. Is there anything that you would wish to add from that report or there is nothing in it that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, it is a very typical example. I chose it because it was fairly untypical -- because it was typical, and there is nothing really more to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could place page 12 of your report onto the ELMO, and this is really for the benefit of the public as well, and this gives quite a neat summary of your findings.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't know if that's in focus or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, that can be clearly seen. Do you have any particular comments on that summary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I'll read it, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you like it read?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could read out your summary of findings.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It's a summary of findings from Kozluk. It's a very large grave site. It had been extensively robbed, but it still contained 292 bodies and 233 body parts. All the victims were apparently male, mostly over the age of 25. Several had old injuries, disabilities, and chronic disease. Blindfolds were found in 13 per cent of bodies, and ligatures in 41 per cent. Eighty-nine per cent of the victims had gunshot injuries, most having been shot either once or twice, but some as many as seven times. The largest number of shots were to the trunk, with the head and legs next, although the commonest final cause of death was gunshot injuries to the head. There were bandaged wounds on two people, suggestive of injuries suffered sometime earlier. There was extensive cutting out, in fact, in many bodies and parts missing. This is the post-mortem damage we spoke about. And the cause of death remained unascertained in a substantial number of people. Some clearly died from causes other than gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you're using a lot of medical terminology, and I wonder, for the sake of the public gallery, could you explain what you mean by "post-mortem", "ante-mortem", and "pari-mortem"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I use only two terms, "post-mortem" and "ante-mortem". Others still use "pari-mortem". "Post-mortem" remains anything occurring after death. "Ante-mortem" is anything occurring before death.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're now going to move to a new site, so I don't know if you want me to continue -- I know the interpreters have been working very hard -- or whether you wish to conclude at this point. It is entirely up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think it is preferable, for it's almost 2.30, so it would be a better idea to resume tomorrow so as to not interrupt the sequence of the testimony. Therefore, Dr. Clark, we expect you to come again tomorrow, please. So we'll be here tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
